items: `$?` = status of the ==most recent foreground command==
One slot only — it is **overwritten**, never stacked
A function call sets it from its `return` or last command
A log line between call and test destroys the status

blocks.title: Capture, then act
blocks.text: `$?` survives exactly __one__ command. Copy it into `rc=$?` on the line right after the call, then branch on `$rc` as often as you like.

blocks.note: trap on the line right after mktemp

items: Set the trap ==immediately==, nothing in between
Single quotes: `$tmp` expands when the trap **fires**
`EXIT` covers return, error, `set -e` and Ctrl-C exits

blocks.title: Where cleanup fails
items: Any command before the trap can abort and leak
Empty `$tmp` plus a trailing slash (`rm -rf "$tmp"/`) targets `/` — guard with `[[ -n $tmp ]] && rm -rf -- "$tmp"`
A second `trap ... EXIT` replaces the first

blocks.title: One line apart
blocks.text: `mktemp` then `trap` with **nothing** between them is the whole pattern. Every command you slip into that gap is a path that can leak.

caption.text: Part 2 of BASH FUNCTIONS FIELD GUIDE. Your Bash function returned a string and the caller got nothing — because `return` only speaks in numbers 0–255, and `local x=$(cmd)` quietly ate the exit code. This handbook is 10 pages on how args arrive, why stdout and status are two separate channels, what dynamic scope really does to your loop counter, and everything a subshell throws away. Save it before the next `cmd | while read` counter mysteriously prints 0.
